subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Functions of families and family forms
Sociological theories of the family (functionalism, Marxism, feminism)

questions.q: According to George Murdock (1949), how many essential functions does the family perform for society?
questions.explain: Murdock argued the family performs four essential functions: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational.

questions.q: Which two functions did the functionalist Talcott Parsons identify as the 'basic and irreducible' functions of the family?
options: Primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of adult personalities
Inheritance of property and social mobility
questions.explain: Parsons claimed the modern nuclear family retains two irreducible functions: primary socialisation of children and the stabilisation of adult personalities.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a nuclear family?
options: Two parents and their dependent children living together
Several generations of relatives living in one household
A step-family formed after divorce or remarriage
A lone parent living with their children
questions.explain: A nuclear family consists of two generations: parents and their dependent children.

questions.q: Which sociologist is associated with the Marxist argument that the family developed to pass on private property through inheritance?
questions.explain: Engels argued the monogamous family emerged so that men could pass on private property to legitimate heirs.

questions.q: Which term did Willmott and Young use to describe the modern family in which partners increasingly share tasks and leisure?
questions.explain: Willmott and Young claimed the family had become 'symmetrical', with partners sharing housework, childcare and leisure more equally.

questions.q: Elizabeth Bott distinguished between which two types of conjugal roles?
questions.explain: Bott identified joint conjugal roles (shared tasks) and segregated conjugal roles (clearly separated tasks).

questions.q: Which feminist sociologist studied housework and challenged the claim that the family had become equal?
questions.explain: Ann Oakley researched housework and argued women still carried the main domestic burden, disputing the symmetrical family.

questions.q: A reconstituted family is best described as a family that is:
options: Formed when partners with children from previous relationships live together
Made up of grandparents, parents and children in one house
Composed of a couple with no children
questions.explain: A reconstituted (step) family is created when adults form a new partnership bringing children from previous relationships.

questions.q: Why do functionalists argue the nuclear family is beneficial to society?
options: It socialises children into shared norms and values
It exploits workers for the ruling class
It prevents social change from occurring
questions.explain: Functionalists see the family as vital because it transmits society's shared norms and values to the next generation.

questions.q: According to Marxists, how does the family benefit capitalism?
options: It reproduces and maintains a workforce that accepts inequality
It ensures men and women share domestic tasks equally
It removes the need for private property
It provides free healthcare for workers
questions.explain: Marxists argue the family reproduces labour power and socialises children to accept a hierarchical, unequal society.

questions.q: Why do feminists argue that the family is patriarchal?
options: It is organised in ways that benefit men and disadvantage women
It treats men and women completely equally
It has no impact on gender roles
It benefits children at the expense of adults
questions.explain: Feminists see the family as patriarchal because women often perform unpaid domestic labour that benefits men.

questions.q: In Parsons' view of conjugal roles, what does the 'expressive' role involve?
options: Providing emotional support and nurturing within the home
Being the main financial provider for the family
Making all decisions about family finances
Working long hours in paid employment
questions.explain: Parsons saw the expressive role, traditionally taken by women, as providing emotional care and warmth, contrasted with the male instrumental (breadwinner) role.

questions.q: What does the 'march of progress' view of family life suggest?
options: Family life is gradually becoming fairer and more equal over time
Family life is getting steadily worse for everyone
The family has not changed at all in modern times
The family will soon disappear completely
questions.explain: The march of progress view, linked to Willmott and Young, argues family relationships have steadily become more equal and companionate.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'dark side' of the family?
options: Harm such as domestic violence and abuse occurring within families
The financial cost of raising children
The decline in the number of extended families
The stress of paid work outside the home
questions.explain: The 'dark side' refers to conflict, abuse and domestic violence, which critics say functionalists ignore.

questions.q: Which description best fits a 'beanpole' family?
options: Several living generations but few members in each generation
A large number of children in a single generation
A couple who choose to have no children
A family with only one parent present
questions.explain: A beanpole family is long and thin: many generations alive at once but few relatives within each generation.

questions.q: What is meant by 'primary socialisation'?
options: The family teaching young children basic norms, values and behaviour
The workplace teaching adults new skills
questions.explain: Primary socialisation is the early learning of a society's norms and values, carried out mainly by the family.

questions.q: In the Ahmed household the husband earns the money and never does housework, while the wife does all the cooking, cleaning and childcare. Which concept best describes this?
questions.explain: Clearly separated tasks, with the wife responsible for domestic labour, illustrate segregated conjugal roles.

questions.q: In the Cole household both partners work full-time and share cooking, cleaning and looking after the children. This best reflects:
questions.explain: Sharing paid work and domestic tasks fairly equally is the defining feature of Willmott and Young's symmetrical family.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that advertising pressures families to keep buying the newest products, which keeps the capitalist economy going. Which perspective is this?
questions.explain: The idea that the family acts as a unit of consumption benefiting capitalism is a Marxist argument.

questions.q: A same-sex couple are raising an adopted child together. This household is an example of:
questions.explain: Same-sex parent families are one form of the increasing diversity of family types in modern Britain.

specSource: AQA GCSE Sociology (8192) specification; The Sociology of Families
